preamble: Loss of the voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ] (Semitic ʿayin) without a consonantal trace recurs across Semitic. In Modern Israeli Hebrew ע has merged with א and, like it, is regularly elided, so Tiberian /ʕoˈlɔm/ 'world' is now /(ʔ)oˈlam/. Maltese għ (from Arabic ʕ and ɣ) is no longer pronounced as a consonant and survives only as length on the neighbouring vowel, as in għajn /aːjn ~ ajn/ 'eye'. In Assyrian Neo-Aramaic ʿayin is a marginal phoneme kept mainly in formal or religious speech; in many dialects it is deleted, as in Nineveh Plains [ʔarba] 'four' beside Standard [ʔarbəʕaː].

examples.note: ע has been absorbed by /ʔ/, which is itself optional; word-initially the consonant is usually not pronounced.
The glottal consonants, including ע, tend to be elided, most often in unstressed syllables and in informal speech also in stressed ones.
The pharyngeal is lost; the archaic variant /aˤːjn/ shows the intermediate pharyngealised long vowel that it left behind.
Archaic /ˈaˤːʃ.ra/; modern Maltese keeps only the length of the vowel.
ʿAyin is deleted, or realised as a vowel, glide or gemination, in most Suret dialects; it is kept mainly in formal or religious speech.
